lesson.title: What a Circuit Feels Like From the Driving Side: Input Resistance
lesson.summary: Input resistance is the equivalent resistance a circuit presents to whatever drives its input terminals, and a high input resistance is usually what protects a signal source from being loaded down.
lesson.body:
Input resistance, written R_in, is the resistance you would measure or calculate looking into a circuit's input terminals, from the point of view of whatever is about to drive it. To find it, you deactivate every independent source inside the circuit, replacing voltage sources with short circuits and current sources with open circuits, then find the equivalent resistance seen from those input terminals. That is the exact same source deactivation procedure used to find a Thevenin resistance, just applied at the input side of a circuit rather than the output side. Input resistance is a property of the circuit itself, it does not depend at all on what eventually gets plugged into it.

Take a simple resistive input network: R1 = 20 kilo ohm and R2 = 5 kilo ohm both connected from the single input terminal to ground, a common arrangement for biasing an amplifier's input stage. Looking into the input terminal, these two resistors are in parallel with each other, so R_in = (20 times 5) divided by (20 plus 5), which is 100 divided by 25, or 4 kilo ohm.

Why this number matters becomes clear once you connect a real source to it. Suppose a sensor behaves like an ideal 5V source with its own output resistance R_s = 1 kilo ohm, driving this 4 kilo ohm input. The two resistances form a voltage divider, so the voltage actually delivered to the input is V_in = V_s times R_in divided by (R_s plus R_in), which is 5V times 4 divided by 5, or 4V. Only 1V, twenty percent of the original signal, is lost across the source's own resistance.

Now compare a poorly designed input stage with R_in = 1 kilo ohm, equal to the source's own resistance. The delivered voltage becomes 5V times 1 divided by 2, or 2.5V, exactly half the original signal, simply because the input resistance was not large enough relative to what was driving it. This is exactly why amplifier and instrument designers push hard for a high input resistance relative to whatever source will typically be connected: it is the single design choice that determines how much of a signal actually survives the connection.

Input resistance depends only on the resistors, and any other passive elements, inside the circuit being measured, found the same way any Thevenin resistance is found. This chapter has looked at it from the driving side of a connection. The next chapter looks at the matching idea from the opposite side, the output resistance of whatever is doing the driving, and the chapter after that, loading effect, puts the two together to explain exactly how much of a signal gets lost whenever any real source meets any real load.

It is worth being precise about what input resistance is not. It is not the same as the resistance of any single component sitting at the input, and it is not necessarily a constant for every circuit, some active circuits present a different input resistance depending on operating conditions. For a purely resistive network like the one above, though, it reduces to exactly the same equivalent resistance calculation covered in earlier chapters, applied at a specific pair of terminals chosen because that is where a future source will connect. Naming it input resistance rather than just equivalent resistance is really a statement of intent about how that number will be used next, to predict how much of an incoming signal survives.
